title: Knowledge Check 7 - Lessons 31-36
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 31-36 - Access to Other Data | Implications of Security Model Choice. Pass with 80% or higher to move toward unlocking the cert prep exam.

questions.question: A Big Object stores two years of historical transaction logs for analysts. How should access be governed?
options: Object-level permissions via profile/permission sets, since Big Objects don't support the full OWD/sharing-rule/role model
OWD to Private plus sharing rules
questions.explanation: Big Objects are optimized for large-scale query and do not support the granular OWD/sharing/role model of standard objects; you govern them with object permissions and design data partitioning. The other options assume standard-object sharing that Big Objects lack.

questions.question: An External Object surfaces data from a partner's system. Who ultimately enforces record-level access to that data?
options: The external data source's own authentication/authorization, with the internal external-object permissions gating who can query at all
A sharing rule on the external object
questions.explanation: External Objects connect to external data; the external system enforces the record-level rules, while internal profile permissions control who may query the external object at all. Internal sharing rules/OWD cannot secure externally-held data.

questions.question: Why must access to Event Monitoring logs be tightly restricted?
options: Audit logs reveal query patterns and data-access behavior that is itself sensitive exposure
questions.explanation: Event monitoring logs capture who queried what and how - exposing them reveals data-access patterns and potential vulnerabilities, so access must be limited to designated admins/analysts.

questions.question: Which sharing design is MOST likely to cause sharing-table bloat on large data volumes?
options: A restrictive OWD with a few sharing rules to groups
Deep role hierarchy with every record gaining an ancestor row, plus large per-record teams
One criteria rule to a single group
questions.explanation: Deep hierarchies and broad per-record teams each add a share row per granted ancestor/member, multiplying across records. Restrictive OWD with a few group rules keeps the table lean.

questions.question: Why can sharing recalculation be expensive at scale?
options: It rebuilds/validates many share rows across large volumes and can be slow and lock-heavy
questions.explanation: Recalculation recomputes the sharing table for many records; on LDV this is CPU/IO heavy, slow, and can lock tables - so designs should minimize recalc frequency.

questions.question: When does a sharing model 'stop scaling' and force a redesign?
options: When OWD is set to Public
When fine-grained per-record access is required for a very large record/user population, multiplying share rows beyond acceptable performance
When a single rule is created
questions.explanation: Per-record grants (teams, manual, Apex shares) over huge populations multiply share rows until performance degrades - at that point you revisit the requirement, the mechanism, or partition the data.

questions.question: An object holds 50M records and needs three analyst groups to each see a subset by region. What is the most scalable design?
options: Three criteria-based sharing rules (one per region) to the three groups, with a restrictive OWD
questions.explanation: A restrictive OWD plus three coarse criteria rules produces few, group-level share rows - the leanest scalable design. Teams/manual shares/hierarchy would create per-record rows across 50M records.

questions.question: How should an architect avoid expensive sharing recalculation on a large object?
options: Base criteria rules on stable fields, batch ownership changes, and schedule necessary recalcs
questions.explanation: Designing rules on stable fields and batching changes minimizes recalculation. Frequent recalcs, hourly recalc, or disabling sharing are not sound approaches.

questions.question: Why does sharing-table bloat degrade query performance even on indexed fields?
options: A bloated sharing table weakens the efficiency of the sharing-model joins/queries and can exceed practical index benefits
questions.explanation: Queries must resolve sharing through the sharing table; when it grows enormously, even indexed lookups slow down and the cost of the sharing join dominates - keeping it lean preserves performance.

questions.question: A permission set grants access to a premium object, but assignment to a standard user produces an error. What is the root cause?
options: The user's license does not support the premium feature the permission set depends on
questions.explanation: Premium-object access is license-gated; the permission set requires an underlying license the user doesn't hold, so assignment fails or the feature is hidden. Sharing/OWD/FLS are unrelated to the license error.

questions.question: Which scenario is most likely a LICENSE limitation rather than a sharing-configuration error?
options: A feature like Experience Cloud, Shield encryption, or Field Audit Trail being unavailable for the org/users
A criteria rule not sharing a record
A page layout missing a field
questions.explanation: Enterprise-grade features (Experience, Shield, Field Audit Trail) are licensed; their absence for users is typically a license-tier limitation, whereas the other options are config/behavior issues.

questions.question: Why can't a permission set grant a capability to a user who lacks the supporting license?
options: Object/system permissions in a permission set must be compatible with the user's single assigned license, and feature gating blocks incompatible grants
questions.explanation: Each user has one license; permission-set grants must be compatible with it, and license-gated features cannot be granted without the supporting license - the permission set cannot bypass the user's license.

questions.question: An org with only internal Salesforce CRM licenses must give partners portal access to their accounts. What is the key licensing implication?
options: Experience/community licenses (e.g. Partner Community) are required for external users and sharing sets; without them portal access is not possible
questions.explanation: External-user portal access is an Experience Cloud (community) feature requiring the corresponding licenses. Without them, sharing sets/portal access cannot be configured; Shield/Platform licenses do not provide it.

questions.question: An architect proposes Field Audit Trail for 5-year retention. Which license is required?
questions.explanation: Field Audit Trail is a Shield (compliance) feature; it requires the Shield license, independent of the sharing configuration. A permission set cannot grant it without the license.

questions.question: Why must sharing-set-based access be flagged as a licensing concern before design?
options: Sharing sets are an Experience Cloud feature requiring external-user licenses, so internal-only orgs must buy those licenses to use them
questions.explanation: Sharing sets are an Experience Cloud capability for external users; an internal-only license inventory cannot deliver partner access through them without purchasing Experience licenses - a licensing constraint on the design.

questions.question: What is the most reliable way to verify a sharing model before rollout?
options: Log in as representative users from each access class and assert their view/edit per record via a test matrix
Only test as the system admin
questions.explanation: A per-user-class test matrix with runAs/login-as assertions verifies both granted and denied access. Testing as admin alone or trusting summaries misses per-class bugs.

questions.question: How can an architect validate the COMPOSITION of a record's effective sharing?
options: Open the record's Sharing detail to see the share-graph rows and their sources (OWD, hierarchy, rules, teams, Apex)
questions.explanation: The Sharing detail lists the share rows and their RowCause/source, revealing exactly which mechanism grants access - essential to catch unexpected grants. Folders, profiles, and backups do not show this.

questions.question: Why must recalculation paths be part of security testing?
options: Criteria changes, ownership transfers, and rule edits can leave stale or missing grants that only recalculation testing surfaces
Recalc is automatic and always correct
questions.explanation: Testing recalculation catches stale (or missing) share rows after the conditions rules depend on change. Recalc is not cosmetic or always-correct - it must be exercised and validated.
